title: Studying Abroad in the United States and Australia
paragraphs: Introduction I was allowed to study abroad at Tulane University in the United States and the University of Western Australia in Australia. Although it was a short period of three months, I was able to experience healthcare in two countries, and it became a very fulfilling clerkship.

Clerkship at Tulane University My honest feeling, looking back, is that I am glad I was able to do the four weeks of clerkship safely. The study abroad at Tulane University was a series of troubles from the preparation stage until the clerkship began. Although I had originally been scheduled for a three-month clerkship, I was told that accepting me would be difficult and the clerkship nearly disappeared, and after I arrived in the United States, communication between the Tulane University administration and the doctors of the clerkship department had not been properly carried out, and the clerkship department refused to accept me. However, I think that such experiences are also part of studying abroad and led to growth as a person.

Clerkship in the MICU Having been refused by the department where I was scheduled, I contacted the administration at a loss, and somehow obtained permission to do my clerkship in pulmonology. Then, when I nervously visited pulmonology on the first day, the attending told me that there were few patients and that the clerkship in the MICU would be more instructive, so I ended my pulmonology clerkship after half a day and ended up in the MICU. In the first week of the finally decided MICU clerkship, partly because I had no authority over the charts, I spent several days following the residents around. I negotiated many times, but in the end I could not obtain chart authority. However, as a result of consulting a fellow, I was allowed to take charge of patients. This experience made me feel in person the words of my seniors that, in studying abroad, it is important to convey your own opinion to the other person firmly and negotiate. The clerkship in the MICU basically consisted of making rounds on my assigned patients every morning and evening, asking the nurses about the patients' condition and vital signs overnight, asking the local students and residents every day to show me the test data and charts, and presenting at the attending rounds. The rounds ran from 8:30 to 12:00 or 13:00, and on those occasions I was given assignments such as the difference between massive PE and submassive PE and the Berlin definition of ARDS. In the clerkship I was basically treated the same as the local students. Being treated as an equal made me confront even more the gap with the local students and the language barrier, and I felt frustrated many times. For example, while the local students were able to elicit more from patients than I could in presentations on rounds and built good relationships with patients and doctors through small talk and so on, there were times when I could not completely hear what the other person was saying. Under those circumstances I thought about what I could do, and I visited my patients more often than the local students did, resigned myself to the fact that being Japanese it could not be helped and asked questions when there was something I did not understand, and looked up papers and presented them. I was very happy that on one day's presentation the attending said "Well done!" In the MICU I was also able to experience many cases that one cannot experience much in Japan. Because it is in the southern United States and is the region with the most HIV and tuberculosis patients in the country, there were patients with sickle cell disease, Pneumocystis pneumonia and MAC disease due to HIV, and even a patient with Good syndrome, a rare immunodeficiency. After the rounds I took part in Grand Rounds and took histories with local students in the clinic at UMC, a state hospital. At Grand Rounds, enjoying an American lunch of pizza and cola, I was able to learn about the treatment of IBD and diagnosis by echo. At the clinic, there were many Medicaid patients, and there were things that made me think, such as restrictions on drugs during treatment. What left the greatest impression in those four weeks was a patient with Guillain-Barre syndrome who was admitted in the first week of the clerkship and discharged in the last week. On admission the patient was intubated and we communicated with an alphabet board and nodding of the neck, but even after extubation the paralysis did not improve right away, and on days when the patient was in a bad mood, they sometimes did not answer much even when I asked questions. However, as the condition improved, conversation increased, and when leaving the hospital the patient said to me, "Sometimes I was in a bad mood because I couldn't move my body because of the illness, but thank you so much. Do your best when you go back to Japan," and I felt that I might have been able to do something for the patient.

Clerkship at the University of Western Australia After finishing the clerkship in the United States, I set off on a 35-hour journey from New Orleans to Perth. During the transit in Hong Kong, seeing Asian people and kanji for the first time in a month, I remember I became a little homesick for Japan. The dispatch to UWA was originally scheduled to begin next fiscal year, but because the clerkship period at Tulane University was shortened, it was suddenly decided that I would be sent from this fiscal year. UWA is a university in The Group of Eight, which is positioned like the former Imperial Universities of Japan, and Professor Barry Marshall, who discovered H. pylori and won the Nobel Prize, and others are on its staff. At UWA I did clerkships at the major hospitals in Perth. I rotated through the Acute Surgical Unit at Fiona Stanley Hospital and the Transplant Unit at Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital.

Clerkship in the Acute Surgical Unit Fiona Stanley Hospital is a new and very beautiful hospital located about an hour south of the center of Perth by public transport. The ASU clerkship began with paper round at 7:00 in the morning, followed by ward rounds. After the ward rounds I observed or assisted in operations. The operations were mainly common ones such as cholecystitis, appendicitis, small bowel obstruction and hernia, and there was even a day when I assisted in five appendicectomies in a row, so in four weeks I was allowed to scrub into really many operations. After taking part in the rounds, it was basically "It's up to you," so it was a clerkship where it was fine to scrub into operations or take a break, but I thought it would be a waste of this opportunity, so I became friends with medical students from UWA and the University of Notre Dame, was allowed to take part in their seminars, and was allowed to observe operations in other departments.

Clerkship in the Transplant Unit Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital, where I did the clerkship, was a very large hospital with a long history (one might say old) close to the center of Perth. The transplant surgery department was a department rich in international color, as if symbolizing Australia's diversity, and there were doctors from various countries such as China, Malaysia and Germany. Partly because I was very fortunate with the doctors, it became a very fulfilling clerkship. There were ward rounds at 7:30 every morning, and on some days there were radiology and transplant meetings, but basically on days with operations I took part in the operations, assisting or observing. The operations included not only kidney and liver transplants but also, as general surgery, AV fistula creation, PD catheter insertion, lap chole and hernia repair. On days without operations, I sometimes took part in lectures for interns, drew blood, or was allowed to write discharge summaries, and sometimes I followed a consultant and observed the clinic. I was allowed to scrub into about five or six transplant operations in four weeks, and since one cannot know when and where transplants will occur, I once received a phone call while I was at the beach on a holiday. What left an impression was an operation in which the kidneys of a brain-dead adult were transplanted simultaneously into two children. This operation was performed with the whole transplant surgery team traveling to a children's hospital called Princess Margaret Hospital, and it was very moving to see the adult kidney, white before transplantation, turn red inside the small body of the child after transplantation.

Finally My honest impression is that I am truly glad I studied abroad. I met many people, came into contact with human kindness, and met wonderful people whom I could respect and wanted to become like myself. Through the three months of study abroad I was able to experience not only differences in healthcare such as medical systems and how doctors work, but also many other things such as differences in religion and culture. I strongly felt anew that just being able to speak English expands my world this much, and I thought that if I have the chance to study abroad in the future I would like to take up the challenge again. I am grateful to my parents who supported my study abroad, and to the classmates who went abroad with me, especially 井上 and 中村, with whom I lined up beds in a small room and shared life. And that I was given such a valuable experience this time is thanks to the people of the International Collaboration Office, starting with Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川, Ms. 西尾, and the seniors of the Frontier Association who laid the foundations of study abroad. I am sincerely grateful. Thank you very much.
